newsitem.title: FRANCE: French turnout up from last election at midday.
newsitem.headline: French turnout up from last election at midday.

text.p: Voting in the first round of France's parliamentary election got off faster than in the last 1993 poll on Sunday, with President Jacques Chirac seeking a renewed centre-right majority until the year 2002.
The Interior Ministry said turnout by midday (1000 GMT) was 22.74 percent. At the last election in 1993, turnout was 21.4 percent at midday but by the end of polling totalled 69.1 percent.

Opinion polls before a publication blackout a week ago showed the ruling centre-right coalition led by Chirac's allies was likely to win most seats in the 577-member National Assembly but that the Socialist-led opposition was in striking distance of an upset.
A runoff will be held on June 1 in constituencies where no candidate wins the 50 percent needed to win a seat outright. First-round turnout in 1993 was the second lowest on record.

An overall low turnout might help Prime Minister Alain Juppe by cutting the number of three-way runoffs involving the far-right National Front of Jean-Marie Le Pen, whose voters tend to pick the centre-right if their candidate is eliminated.

Candidates need the support of 12.5 percent of all registered voters to reach the second round. That means that if turnout matches that of 1993, a candidate would need 18 percent of the votes cast to reach the second round.
